title: Responsible Use of AI — Learning Module
description: Required learning: using AI tools safely, lawfully and accountably at Opal.
content:
# Responsible Use of AI — Learning Module

This module is required for all staff before client-facing work. It pairs with the Responsible Use of AI Policy, and ends with a short knowledge check (pass mark 80 per cent, unlimited attempts).

## 1. Accountability

AI can draft; only a clinician can be responsible. Whatever role a tool played, the clinician who signs a note, report or letter owns every word of it — its accuracy, its tone, its clinical claims. "The AI wrote that part" is not a sentence that exists in professional practice. AI is never the responsible clinician.

## 2. Human review, always

Every AI-drafted clinical artefact is reviewed, corrected and approved by the responsible clinician before it enters a record or leaves the practice. Review means actually reading it — line by line, against what you know of the session — not skimming for obvious errors. If reviewing takes as long as writing would have, that is sometimes the honest cost.

## 3. Privacy

Identifiable participant information goes only into tools the practice owner has approved for that purpose. Unapproved tools — consumer chatbots, free transcription sites, browser extensions — may retain, train on, or expose what you paste. The test is simple: if you would not read it aloud in a shopping centre, do not paste it into an unapproved tool. Breaches here are data breaches and are handled as such.

## 4. Consent and transparency

If a session is recorded or transcribed by an AI tool, the participant knows, in plain language, before it happens — and their consent is documented. "The system was listening the whole time" is not a conversation you ever want to have after the fact.

## 5. Limitations and hallucination

AI systems generate fluent, confident text that can be flatly wrong: invented scores, misremembered dates, plausible-sounding clinical claims with no basis in your session. Fluency is not accuracy. Verify every fact, figure, name and clinical assertion. Treat AI drafts the way you would treat a keen student's draft: useful, and not yet trustworthy.

## 6. Bias

AI reflects its training data, which contains the biases of the world. Watch for deficit-framing, stigmatising descriptions, cultural assumptions and gendered language in generated text. Opal's person-first, strengths-based standard applies to machine drafts exactly as it does to human ones — and machine drafts fail it more often.

## 7. The line that does not move

AI may summarise, structure, draft and translate jargon into plain language. It does not make clinical decisions. Assessment conclusions, recommendations, risk judgements and anything resembling a diagnosis are made by clinicians, with AI at most organising the material the clinician has already judged.

## Completing this module

Complete the knowledge check to record your completion. Then acknowledge the Responsible Use of AI Policy if you have not already. Questions or edge cases — a tool you want approved, a use you are unsure about — go to the practice owner before use, not after.

content:
# Emotional Regulation — Intervention Guide

Emotional regulation work at Opal starts from one commitment: **regulation is a developmental capacity we help build, not a behaviour we extract.** The goal is a person who can weather and recover from big feelings with the right support — never a quieter, more convenient child. If an intervention's real success measure is adult convenience, it is not our intervention.

## Reframe the referral

Referrals often arrive as behaviour complaints: meltdowns, refusal, aggression. Translate before treating: behaviour is communication and overflow. The clinical questions are — what is this nervous system carrying, what skills are still developing, what in the environment exceeds current capacity, and what does support look like?

## Assess the whole picture

- **Regulation demands:** map the day for demand peaks — transitions, sensory load, social complexity, hunger, fatigue. Patterns usually explain more than diagnoses do.
- **Sensory contribution:** many regulation difficulties have a sensory processing dimension — see Sensory Regulation. Assess rather than assume.
- **Co-regulation available:** regulation develops through co-regulation. Assess what the adults around the child have capacity for — and what they need themselves.
- **The child's experience:** ask, at their level. Children often know exactly what overwhelms them; nobody has asked without an agenda before.

## Intervention: bodies before strategies, connection before content

1. **Reduce the mismatch first.** Adjust environments and demands so the child spends more time within capacity — regulation skills are learnt in the regulated zone, not during flooding. This is not "lowering expectations"; it is building the training conditions.
2. **Build co-regulation.** Coach the key adults in reading early signs, lending calm (voice, pace, proximity), and connecting before correcting. An adult's regulation is the intervention the child borrows.
3. **Grow body awareness.** Interoception work — noticing the body's signals with curiosity, without judgement — underpins self-regulation. Playful, concrete, never a test.
4. **Introduce strategies as tools the child owns.** Breathing, movement breaks, retreat spaces and sensory tools are offered, practised when calm, and framed as the child's own kit — not imposed mid-crisis, and never contingent on "good behaviour". A retreat space a child is sent to is a punishment; one they choose is a skill.
5. **Practise recovery, not just prevention.** Coming back from dysregulation — repair, re-entry, no shame — is a skill families and classrooms can learn as a routine.

## Language matters clinically

Notes and reports describe regulation development and support needs — "became overwhelmed during the transition and needed ten minutes of co-regulation to recover" — not compliance vocabulary ("non-compliant", "attention-seeking", "manipulative"). The record shapes how every future reader treats this child.

## Escalate what is beyond scope

Regulation difficulties entangled with trauma, self-harm, or risk to others need coordinated care — bring these to supervision early, refer where indicated, and use the Clinical Escalation Pathway for anything urgent.

# Rural Clinical Planning

In metropolitan practice, a forgotten item costs a return trip. In rural practice, it can cost a month. Rural clinical work rewards ruthless planning.

## Plan the circuit, then the visits

Start with geography: which families, which towns, what order, how long at each. Then plan each visit inside that frame. A good circuit trades a little travel efficiency for clinical sensibility — do not schedule your most demanding assessment at the end of a 400 km day.

## Every visit earns its drive

For each visit, be able to answer: what will be different after this visit? Rural visits should be planned as high-density contacts — assessment plus coaching plus equipment review in one session, with the priorities ranked in advance so that if the session shrinks, the most important work still happens.

## Pack for the plan, and its failure

- Assessment materials for the planned work, plus the one assessment you might plausibly need if presentation has changed.
- Intervention and coaching materials that can stay with the family — home programs, visual supports — because you will not be back next week.
- Equipment: everything to be trialled, fitted, adjusted or retrieved, checked against the trip plan before departure. Chargers, spare parts, basic tools.
- Consent forms and any paperwork needing signatures — chasing signatures remotely is slow.

## Build the between-visit plan

The circuit ends; the therapy should not. Before leaving each family: agree what happens until next contact, who does it, and how it will be supported — telehealth review booked, phone coaching scheduled, school contacted. Write the next-contact plan into the note the same evening.

## Local partnerships

Schools, community health, Aboriginal health services and local support workers multiply what a visiting therapist can achieve — with consent, brief them on the plan and what to watch for. A local pair of hands between circuits is often worth more than an extra visit.

## Document on the road

Notes are written the evening of the visit, on the trip, while detail is fresh. A circuit's documentation completed after returning home is a week late and half the quality.

content:
# Ahpra Shared Code of Conduct — Summary

The shared Code of conduct applies to occupational therapists and most other registered health professions. It describes the professional behaviour and conduct expected by the National Boards. This is a working summary; the code itself is the authority.

## Core expectations

1. **Put patients first — safe, effective and collaborative practice.** Good care is the primary duty: practise safely, within scope and competence, and collaborate with the person and their supports.
2. **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health and cultural safety.** Cultural safety is defined by the recipient of care. Practitioners are expected to provide care free of racism, and to reflect on their own biases and practice.
3. **Respectful and culturally safe practice for all.** Respect for every patient's culture, identity and experience; care that is free of discrimination.
4. **Working with patients.** Informed consent, effective communication, privacy and confidentiality, appropriate professional boundaries — including the strict prohibition on sexual boundary violations.
5. **Working with other practitioners.** Respectful collegial conduct, safe handover, and never disparaging colleagues in ways that undermine care.
6. **Working within the healthcare system.** Wise stewardship of resources; honest, accurate documentation and certificates; lawful billing.
7. **Minimising risk to patients.** Recognising and acting on risk, including your own health, fatigue and impairment; mandatory notification obligations where required: Requires legal/regulatory verification.

# Privacy and Confidentiality Policy

## Purpose

Opal Therapy holds sensitive health information about participants and personal information about staff. This policy sets the standard for collecting, using, storing and disclosing that information.

## Principles

1. **Collect the minimum.** We collect only the information needed for safe, effective therapy and lawful practice administration.
2. **Use for purpose.** Information collected for therapy is used for therapy, its administration and its funding — nothing else without consent.
3. **Disclose deliberately.** Disclosure outside the care team requires participant consent, except where the law requires or permits disclosure (for example, mandatory reporting or serious threat). Where obligations depend on registration status or jurisdiction: Requires legal/regulatory verification.
4. **Store securely.** Client information lives in approved practice systems only — never in personal email, personal cloud storage, unapproved apps or unattended paper.
5. **Speak carefully.** No identifying discussion of participants in public places, group chats or social settings. De-identify case discussions in supervision beyond the care team where practicable.

## Practical rules

- Lock devices whenever unattended; use unique passwords and screen locks.
- Confirm the recipient before sending anything containing client information; email misdirection is our most likely breach.
- Paper travelling to community visits is minimised, carried out of sight and returned or destroyed securely.
- Photographs and recordings require documented consent and are stored only in approved systems.
- Participants may request access to their information; route requests to the practice owner.

## Breach response

Any suspected privacy breach — lost device, misdirected email, unauthorised access — is reported to the practice owner the same day. See the Data Breach Response Policy. Notification obligations under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: Requires legal/regulatory verification.

## Accountability

All staff acknowledge this policy on commencement and after each material change. Breaches are managed under the Incident Management Policy and may constitute misconduct.

description: Assessing activities of daily living across settings and support levels.
content:
# ADL Assessment — Overview

Activities of daily living — personal care, feeding, mobility within the home, toileting, dressing, hygiene — are where independence is most personal. Assessing them well is equal parts method and tact.

## Method

1. **Interview first, observe second.** Start with the person's account of a typical day, then observe the tasks that matter most to the referral question — performed where and when they really happen, morning routines especially.
2. **Record support level per task, not overall.** The useful finding is granular: independent with setup for upper-body dressing, physical assistance for lower-body; supervision for shower transfers because of one step. Blanket ratings hide exactly what plans need to know.
3. **Note the difference between capacity and habit.** Some tasks are done for the person by routine rather than necessity. Distinguish "cannot", "does not currently" and "has never had the chance" — each points to a different intervention.
4. **Capture fluctuation and fatigue.** ADL performance at 7 am after a bad night is the performance that determines support needs.
5. **Use standardised measures within competence where they add structure** (see the Assessment Tool Directory), and let observation lead.

## Tact

ADL assessment enters bathrooms and bedrooms. Explain why, obtain consent for each observed task, offer alternatives (informant report, partial observation) where observation is intrusive, and preserve dignity relentlessly — the assessment is never worth degrading the person it serves.

## Writing it up

Findings run the functional impact chain: task, current performance and support level, consequence for participation and independence, and what would change it. Specific, measured, respectful.

## Purpose

Incidents are inevitable in community practice; unreported incidents are the only unforgivable kind. This policy covers any event that caused, or could have caused, harm to a participant, staff member or other person, plus property and privacy incidents.

## What to report

- Injury or harm to a participant or staff member during service delivery or travel.
- Behavioural incidents, aggression, or threats.
- Medication, equipment or environmental safety events.
- Vehicle incidents on work travel.
- Privacy and security incidents (also see Data Breach Response Policy).

## How to report

1. Make people safe first; use the Clinical Escalation Pathway for urgent clinical risk.
2. Tell the practice owner by phone the same day for anything involving harm or serious risk.
3. Complete a written incident report within 24 hours: factual, timed, first-person, distinguishing observation from interpretation.
4. Record the clinical dimensions in the participant's record where the incident involved a participant.

Certain serious incidents connected with NDIS supports carry external notification obligations to the NDIS Commission, with strict timeframes. Whether and how these apply to Opal's circumstances: Requires legal/regulatory verification — escalate to the practice owner immediately rather than resolving alone.

## Learning

Every incident ends in a documented review with actions and owners. Reviews focus on systems before individuals: the question is "what made this likely?", not "who do we blame?".

Telehealth extends access — particularly for rural and remote participants — when it is clinically appropriate and delivered to the same standard as in-person care.

# Professional Boundaries Policy

## Purpose

Community-based practice puts therapists inside homes and family life. That privilege demands clearer boundaries than clinic practice, not looser ones.

## Standards

1. **The relationship is therapeutic.** Friendship, romantic or sexual relationships with participants or their close family members are prohibited. Ahpra and OT Board expectations apply throughout: see the Shared Code of Conduct summary in the Resource Hub.
2. **Gifts.** Token gifts of trivial value may be accepted graciously and disclosed to the practice owner. Money, significant gifts, bequests or loans are declined.
3. **Contact channels.** Client contact happens through practice channels — practice phone and email — within reasonable hours. Personal social media connections with participants or their families are not accepted.
4. **Self-disclosure.** Brief, purposeful self-disclosure that serves the participant's goals can be appropriate; venting, over-sharing or seeking support from participants is not.
5. **Physical contact** is limited to what the therapy task requires, explained beforehand, and delivered with consent.
6. **Dual relationships.** In small and rural communities, overlap is sometimes unavoidable. Disclose any dual relationship to the practice owner and plan how it will be managed rather than pretending it away.
7. **Finances.** Therapists do not handle participant money, witness wills, or act as advocates in financial matters.

## When lines blur

Boundary drift is gradual by nature. If you notice yourself making exceptions for one participant, extending sessions socially, or dreading disclosure of some interaction in supervision — that is the signal. Raise it in supervision early; early conversations are routine, late ones are incidents.

Writing Functional Impact
description: The chain from diagnosis to support requirement, with worked examples.
content:
# Writing Functional Impact

Reports fail most often at one point: the gap between a diagnosis and a support recommendation, crossed with a hand-wave. Functional impact writing is how that gap gets bridged with reasoning a reader can follow and a delegate can rely on.

## The chain

Every functional impact statement walks five links:

**Diagnosis → impairment → functional impact → participation consequence → support requirement**

- **Diagnosis** names the condition.
- **Impairment** names what the condition affects in this person — the specific body function or structure.
- **Functional impact** names what the impairment does to activity performance — observed and measured where possible.
- **Participation consequence** names what that costs the person in daily life: the roles, routines and settings affected.
- **Support requirement** names what is needed to close the gap, and why this support at this intensity.

A reader should be able to run a finger down the chain and never encounter a leap. If any link is missing, the recommendation is an assertion, not an argument.

## Worked example one — paediatric

> **Diagnosis:** Cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia, GMFCS III).
> **Impairment:** Increased lower-limb muscle tone and reduced selective motor control, with reduced standing balance.
> **Functional impact:** Ruby, aged 7, mobilises indoors with a posterior walker and requires adult assistance for all transfers to and from the floor. She fatigues after approximately 50 metres and cannot manage steps without full assistance. Observed across home and school visits in June 2026; consistent with parent and teacher report.
> **Participation consequence:** Ruby cannot move between her classroom and the library or playground without an adult, which excludes her from unstructured play with peers at recess — the setting where her class friendships are formed. At home she cannot get to the backyard independently.
> **Support requirement:** [The recommendation follows — equipment, environmental modification and therapy, each justified against exactly this picture, with intensity and expected outcome.]

Note what the example does: it measures (50 metres, all transfers), it locates evidence (settings, dates, informants), and its participation consequence is specific and human — recess friendships, the backyard — not "reduced community participation".

## Worked example two — adult

> **Diagnosis:** Schizophrenia, with a significant psychosocial disability.
> **Impairment:** Persistent difficulties with initiation, planning and sustained attention; symptom exacerbation under stress.
> **Functional impact:** Daniel, 34, can complete individual domestic tasks when prompted at each step, but does not initiate them: without prompting, meals are missed and washing accumulates for weeks. He managed two of six planned community outings independently during the assessment month, withdrawing when transport was disrupted. Reported by Daniel and his mother; consistent with observation across four home visits.
> **Participation consequence:** Daniel's tenancy is at risk — two property inspections have failed — and his stated goal of returning to part-time work is blocked less by skills than by the initiation and routine difficulties that also affect his home life.
> **Support requirement:** [Recommendation follows — support intensity and skill-building justified by the initiation picture specifically, with the tenancy and work goals as the outcome frame.]

Note the shape: capability with prompting versus without is the load-bearing distinction for psychosocial disability, and it is stated with numbers and sources, not adjectives.

## Habits that keep the writing honest

1. **Measure what you claim.** Distances, frequencies, prompt levels, durations. "Requires significant support" means nothing a delegate can weigh; "requires verbal prompting at each step of a four-step task" does.
2. **Best day and worst day.** Fluctuating conditions need both described, and the support requirement reasoned against the realistic range, not the best day a review meeting happens to see.
3. **Distinguish won't, can't and hasn't-had-the-chance.** Performance versus capacity versus opportunity — conflating them produces recommendations that miss.
4. **Anchor to the person's goals.** Participation consequences matter because they block this person's stated life, and the report should say so in their words where possible.

content:
# Would We Fund It? — Using the NDIA Guidance

The NDIA publishes "Would we fund it" guidance: worked examples showing how funding criteria apply to real support types — equipment, therapies, everyday items and services. It is one of the most useful public windows into NDIA reasoning, and one of the most misused.

## What it is

Each example walks a support type through the funding considerations: relation to disability, effectiveness and good practice, value for money, and what falls to other systems or ordinary family life. Reading a handful of examples teaches the **shape** of the reasoning faster than any summary.

## What it is not

- **Not a promise.** An example showing a support being funded is never a guarantee for any individual participant — plan circumstances decide, case by case.
- **Not a prohibition.** An example showing a support declined does not make it unfundable for a participant whose circumstances differ materially.
- **Not a substitute for the current guidance.** Examples are updated; always read them live at the source, not from memory or screenshots.

## Using it well at Opal

1. Before recommending an unusual or contested support, read the nearest examples and note how the criteria were weighed.
2. Structure your written justification to answer the same considerations the examples answer — that is the reasoning a delegate applies.
3. Where an example appears to cut against your recommendation, address the difference in circumstances explicitly rather than hoping nobody notices.
4. In conversations with families, use the guidance to explain how decisions are made — while being clear the decision is the NDIA's, not ours.

# How We Work

This is the practical shape of a week at Opal Therapy.

## Scheduling

Your calendar lives in the Opal Portal and can be connected to Outlook. Appointments are booked as single events with a client name, location and session type. Travel is planned around geography — we cluster visits by suburb corridor so that travel time serves the participant, not the map.

## Travel

Community visits are the norm. Log travel in the Travel Logbook as you go, not at the end of the week. For rural and remote trips, complete the Pre-Trip Checklist and follow the Rural and Remote Travel Policy — trip plans, check-ins and vehicle readiness are not optional.

## Documentation

Clinical notes are written the same day wherever possible, and always within the timeframe in the Clinical Documentation Standard. Reports go through a draft-review cycle before they leave the practice. Nothing generated by an AI tool enters a record without clinician review.

## Communication

- Urgent clinical concerns: phone the practice owner directly.
- Same-day scheduling issues: phone or message the admin coordinator.
- Everything else: portal notifications and email, checked at least twice a day.

## Meetings

A short weekly team meeting covers caseload, travel and flags. Supervision is scheduled separately and protected — it is not absorbed by operational talk.

## The rule that holds it together

If you are unsure whether something needs to be escalated, documented or double-checked: it does. See Who to Ask for Help and the Clinical Escalation Pathway.

description: Working effectively inside schools: partnership, participation and practicality.
content:
# School-Based Occupational Therapy

School is where children do their most public occupational performance, six hours a day. Therapy that works there multiplies; therapy that ignores the setting evaporates on the drive home.

## The stance: guest and partner

We are guests in a system with its own expertise, pressures and rhythms. The teacher knows this classroom; we know this child's function. The work succeeds where those meet.

- Book visits through the school's process, sign in, and respect timetables — arriving during assessment week uninvited costs a term of goodwill.
- Establish the consent picture before the first visit: parental consent for the school contact, and clarity about what will be shared with whom.
- Feed back to both teacher and family after every visit, within consent. The child does not benefit from a therapist-teacher channel the family cannot see, nor the reverse.

## Assess participation, not just performance

Classroom observation looks at the child in context: the demands of this classroom, this teacher's style, the desk setup, the playground, transitions, mealtimes. Often the highest-value finding is an environment-task mismatch, not a child deficit — the pencil grip matters less than the fact that handwriting demands peak right after the sensory chaos of lunch.

## Intervene through the setting

1. **Prefer strategies the classroom can absorb.** A two-minute movement break for the whole class survives; a special routine for one child that costs the teacher attention mostly does not. Whole-class wins remove stigma and get maintained.
2. **Coach the adults who are there daily.** Teachers and education assistants deliver more therapy minutes than we ever will — see Caregiver Coaching for the method; it applies to classrooms directly.
3. **Make recommendations implementable by this school.** Equipment that fits the room, strategies that fit the timetable, wording that fits school planning documents. Ask what is feasible rather than prescribing into a vacuum.
4. **Withdraw thoughtfully.** Pull-out sessions have their place (skill acquisition needing low distraction), but the default is building skills where they are used.

## Write for the school audience too

School-facing summaries are short, practical and free of clinical jargon: what helps this child, what to watch for, what to try first when things wobble. One page a relief teacher could act on beats five pages nobody rereads.

## When school and family disagree

It happens: about priorities, about diagnosis, about what the child can do. Hold the child's participation as the shared ground, document perspectives fairly, and avoid becoming either side's advocate against the other — see the Professional Boundaries Policy, and bring persistent conflicts to supervision.

This guide supports clinical reasoning at Opal Therapy. It does not replace professional judgement, supervision, jurisdiction-specific requirements or current official guidance, and it is never a guarantee of any funding outcome.

# Work Health and Safety Policy

## Purpose

Opal's workplace is wherever the work is: vehicles, homes, schools and community venues. Work health and safety duties follow the work, and everyone holds a share of them.

## Responsibilities

- **The practice** provides safe systems of work (this policy suite), consults staff on WHS matters, and acts on reported hazards.
- **All staff** take reasonable care for their own safety and others', follow safety procedures, and report hazards, incidents and near misses promptly.

## Core controls

1. **Travel and driving.** Fatigue management and vehicle standards per the Rural and Remote Travel Policy; seatbelts always; no phone handling while driving — calls wait or route through hands-free.
2. **Manual handling.** Therapy work involves lifting, transfers and equipment. Use taught techniques, ask for help or equipment rather than improvising, and decline manual handling that exceeds safe limits.
3. **Home and community environments.** Assess each environment on entry: trip hazards, animals, smoke, aggression indicators. The Lone Worker Safety Policy applies to all solo visits.
4. **Psychosocial safety.** Workload, exposure to distressing content, and isolation are hazards, not weaknesses. Raise them in supervision or directly with the practice owner; they are managed like any other risk.
5. **First aid and emergencies.** Know the first-aid kit locations (vehicle and office) and keep personal currency in first aid where required for your role.

## Jurisdictional obligations

Specific WHS duties, notifiable incident thresholds and workers' compensation requirements are jurisdiction-dependent: Requires legal/regulatory verification. The practice owner maintains the current position.

# Welcome to Opal Therapy

Welcome. Opal Therapy is a community-based occupational therapy practice serving participants across metropolitan, rural and remote Western Australia. Most of our work happens where life happens: homes, schools, workplaces and community settings, with telehealth extending our reach where distance makes in-person visits impractical.

## What we do

We provide occupational therapy assessment and intervention for NDIS participants and privately funded clients across the lifespan. Typical work includes functional capacity assessments, assistive technology and home modification assessments, school-based therapy, skill-building intervention, and caregiver coaching.

## How we are organised

Opal is deliberately small and low-hierarchy. You will work directly with the practice owner, an admin coordinator, and a team of treating therapists. There is no layer of middle management; questions travel fast and decisions are made close to the work.

## What we expect of you

- Person-first, strengths-based practice in everything you write and do.
- Honest, timely clinical documentation — same-day notes wherever possible.
- Asking early. A five-minute question beats a five-week problem.
- Care for your own safety and wellbeing, especially when travelling.

## What you can expect from us

- A structured first week with a named contact for questions.
- Supervision that is regular, planned and protected.
- Tools that reduce administrative load, including the Opal Portal for scheduling, travel and resources.

content:
# Using the OT Knowledge Library

The OT Knowledge Library is a curated shelf of external links: official NDIA and NDIS Commission guidance, professional bodies, evidence databases and learning platforms. Nothing in it reproduces external content — every entry points you to the source.

## Authority badges

Every resource carries an authority badge. **Official** marks regulators and government agencies (NDIA, NDIS Commission) — the sources that decide things. **Professional Body** marks associations such as OTA, WAOTA, AOTA and RCOT. **External** marks everything else: research groups, evidence databases and training providers, credible but not authoritative. The badge tells you how much weight a source carries in a funding or regulatory question.

## Free, Paid and origin filters

Library entries are tagged **Free** or **Paid** (resources with a substantial free tier are tagged Free, with paid options noted in the entry), and **Australia** or **International** by origin. Use the Cost filter in the Library to browse only free resources — there are many, and they cover most everyday needs.

## The Essentials shortlist

Eighteen entries are tagged **Essential** and surface first in the collection: the free resources with the highest practical value per minute, from the NDIA's FCA and evidence guidance through to the Rehabilitation Measures Database and the living stroke guidelines. If you read nothing else in the library, read these.

## The reporting principle the library serves

Reflecting current NDIA evidence guidance, strong reports walk one unbroken chain: **diagnosis, then impairment, then functional impact, then support need, then proposed support, then expected functional outcome, then why the support is reasonable and necessary.** The NDIA entries in this library are the official statements of what each link requires; the evidence databases are how the "effective and beneficial" link gets its citations.

## The rule that does not bend

External links are pointers, not copies. For any funding, pricing or regulatory decision, always open the official source and rely on what it says today — never on a summary, a memory or a screenshot.

Equipment Trial Guide
description: Running equipment trials that produce a real decision.
content:
# Equipment Trial Guide

An equipment trial exists to answer one question: does this item solve this person's functional problem in this life? Trials that lack a question produce impressions; funded equipment needs findings.

## Before the trial

1. **Define success in writing.** Two to four measurable criteria drawn from the functional need: "independent shower transfer without skin shear", "self-propels the school corridor within passing period", "carer completes the hoist transfer alone, safely". If you cannot state the criteria, the assessment is not finished (see AT Assessment Workflow).
2. **Trial in the real environment** — the actual bathroom, school, vehicle. Showroom trials answer showroom questions.
3. **Set the duration to expose real life.** Long enough for novelty to wear off and routine friction to appear — a single demonstration is not a trial for anything consequential.
4. **Brief every user.** The participant, family and support workers know what is being tested, how to use the item safely, and what to record. Arrange supplier setup and any interim safety measures.

## During the trial

- Record against the criteria, plus: comfort over time, effort and setup burden, fit across all users and routines, storage and transport reality, and the participant's own verdict — an item the person dislikes is a non-solution regardless of function.
- Capture failures precisely (what task, what circumstances) — they steer specification changes.
- Stop the trial early for any safety event; report per the Incident Management Policy.

## After the trial

Decide against the written criteria: met, partially met with specified changes, or not met. Record the outcome either way — documented unsuccessful trials are valuable evidence of options considered, and they belong in the recommendation's justification. Then complete the recommendation per Clinical Recommendations, with quotes and current funding rules checked at the official sources.

This guide supports clinical reasoning at Opal Therapy. It does not replace professional judgement, supervision, jurisdiction-specific requirements or current official guidance, and it is never a guarantee of any funding outcome.

# Information Security Policy

## Purpose

Clinical information is only as secure as the devices and accounts that touch it. These are the practice-wide rules.

## Accounts

1. Unique, strong passwords for every practice system; no password reuse from personal accounts. A password manager is recommended.
2. Multi-factor authentication is enabled wherever the system supports it.
3. Accounts are personal. Credentials are never shared, and work is never done under another person's login.

## Devices

- Any device used for practice work has a screen lock, encryption enabled and current operating system updates.
- Devices are locked whenever unattended, and never left visible in parked vehicles.
- Lost or stolen devices are reported to the practice owner immediately — hours matter. See the Data Breach Response Policy.

## Data handling

- Client information lives in approved practice systems only. No forwarding to personal email, no personal cloud drives, no USB sticks except where the practice owner approves an encrypted device for a specific purpose.
- Public Wi-Fi is not used for practice systems unless connecting through the approved secure method.
- Paper is a device too: minimise it, carry it out of sight, store it locked and destroy it securely.

## Email and messages

Phishing is the most likely attack we will face. Verify unexpected requests for credentials, payment changes or client data by phone before acting. Report suspicious messages to the practice owner rather than deleting them silently.

## Leaving the practice

On departure, access is revoked, practice data is returned or destroyed as directed, and no client information leaves with the departing staff member.

# Conflict of Interest Policy

## Purpose

A conflict of interest exists whenever a personal interest could influence — or reasonably appear to influence — professional judgement. Conflicts are common and manageable; concealed conflicts are neither.

## Common examples

- Recommending equipment or services from a supplier in which a staff member has a financial interest or receives benefits.
- Providing services to family members, friends or close community connections.
- Secondary employment with providers serving the same participants.
- Gifts or hospitality from suppliers beyond trivial value.

## Rules

1. **Disclose early.** Actual, potential and perceived conflicts are disclosed to the practice owner as soon as recognised, and recorded in the practice register.
2. **Manage deliberately.** Management options include disclosure to the participant, reassignment of the client, independent second opinions on recommendations, or declining the interest. The plan is documented.
3. **Recommendations stay clean.** Equipment and provider recommendations are made on clinical merit, with options offered where reasonable. Commissions or referral kickbacks are never accepted.
4. **Small communities.** In rural work, overlapping relationships are normal. The duty is not to avoid all overlap — often impossible — but to name it and manage it transparently.

## Breaches

Failure to disclose a known conflict is a conduct matter. Honest late disclosure is always better received than discovery.

description: What separates a defensible, useful clinical note from an adequate one.
content:
# Clinical Note Quality

A clinical note has three readers: the future you who must recall the episode, the colleague who may take over the care, and the external reader — participant, auditor, tribunal — who may one day weigh what you did. A quality note serves all three without being rewritten for any of them.

## The standard, restated

The Clinical Documentation Standard sets the floor: same-day writing, attribution, factual accuracy, completeness, respectful language, transparent corrections. This guide is about the craft above the floor.

## Specificity is the whole game

Compare:

> "Worked on fine motor skills. Good session."

> "Practised shoelace tying using the two-loop method introduced last session. Jai completed the sequence independently twice of five attempts (previously zero of five), losing the sequence at the crossover step. He stayed with the task eight minutes with one prompt to return. Mum observed the practice sequence and will support daily practice before school."

The second note takes ninety seconds longer and contains everything the first note only gestures at: intervention, dosage, measured response, the specific sticking point, family involvement and the between-session plan. Write the second note.

## Observation before interpretation

State what you saw, then what you make of it, and keep the two visibly separate: "Ella left the table four times during the twenty-minute task (observation). Her exits followed each new task demand, which is consistent with escape-motivated avoidance of fine motor demands (interpretation)." Interpretation without its observation base is opinion; observation without interpretation is a security camera. Notes need both, in that order.

## Person-first, strengths-honest

Person-first and strengths-based language is our standard, and it must remain honest. Recording strengths does not mean softening difficulties — a note that under-describes functional impact fails the participant at their next plan review. Describe difficulty plainly and respectfully: "Marcus requires full physical assistance for all transfers" is respectful; "Marcus is wheelchair-bound and unable to do transfers" is neither accurate nor respectful.

## Quotes carry weight

The participant's own words, marked as quotes, are among the most powerful content a note can hold — for goals ("I want to make my own lunch"), for risk ("some days I don't see the point"), and for consent conversations. Quote sparingly and exactly.

## Risk gets its own line

Every contact note answers the risk question, even when the answer is "no risk concerns observed this contact". A silent note is ambiguous forever; a one-line answer is evidence you looked.

## The plan makes the note actionable

End with what happens next: who does what, before when, and when the next contact is. A note without a plan ends an episode; a note with a plan continues one.

## Common failure modes

1. **The heroic reconstruction** — five notes written Friday afternoon for a week of sessions. Accuracy decays by the hour; write same-day.
2. **The template ghost** — headings completed with boilerplate that could describe any client. If a sentence could sit in any chart, it is not yet a clinical record.
3. **The advocacy note** — written to argue for funding rather than record events. Record honestly; argue in the report, from honest records.
4. **The euphemism spiral** — softening real difficulties until the record no longer supports the support needs it should evidence.

# Professional Indemnity Insurance — What You Need to Know

Professional indemnity insurance (PII) is a registration requirement: occupational therapists must not practise without appropriate PII arrangements in place, whether held personally, through an employer, or a combination.

1. **Cover must match your practice.** Arrangements must be appropriate for the nature and risk of everything you do — including any private work, telehealth, and secondary roles outside Opal. Employer cover typically covers employed work only.
2. **Run-off cover matters.** Claims can arrive years after the event. Ensure your arrangements deal with claims made after you stop practising or change insurer.
3. **Declare honestly.** Registration renewal includes declaring that PII arrangements are in place. That declaration is personal — verify rather than assume.

- Evidence of current PII (your own policy or confirmation of coverage under practice arrangements) is uploaded to your portal profile and kept current; expiry reminders come from the portal.
- Tell the practice owner about any secondary practice or private work so coverage gaps are identified before they matter.
- Any incident that could conceivably become a claim is reported under the Incident Management Policy promptly — late notification can jeopardise cover.

# Telehealth — A Practical Guide

The Telehealth Policy sets the standards. This guide is about delivery: making a screen-mediated session genuinely therapeutic.

## Before the first session

- Confirm clinical suitability honestly — see the policy. Telehealth is a delivery mode, not a compromise to be apologised for, but it has real limits.
- Obtain telehealth-specific consent, including the backup plan: "If the video drops, I will phone you on this number."
- Do a five-minute tech check with the family before session one: platform installed, camera angle workable, audio adequate. This single habit prevents most failed first sessions.

## Setting up each session

- Private room, closed door, neutral background, decent light on your face.
- Confirm at the start: where the participant is physically, who else is present (on and off camera), and an emergency contact for their location.
- Agree the session plan up front — structure carries more of the load on telehealth than in person.

## Making it work clinically

1. **Coach the hands in the room.** Telehealth OT is often parent or carer coaching: you direct, the adult in the room does. Name this explicitly — "You'll be my hands today" — and it becomes the strength of the format rather than its limitation.
2. **Shrink the frame.** Ask for the camera to move to what matters: the pencil grasp, the bathroom doorway, the seating setup. A guided tour beats a wide static shot.
3. **Shorter, sharper.** Attention fatigues faster on screen, especially for children. Plan 30-40 minute sessions with movement breaks, and put the highest-value work early.
4. **Send materials ahead.** Home programs, visuals and printables arrive before the session, so the family is holding them when you coach their use.

## When it is not working

If connection quality or the participant's presentation makes the session clinically ineffective or unsafe, say so, switch to the phone backup or reschedule, and record the limitation in the note. Repeated failures are a signal to change mode, not to persist politely.

## Documentation

Same standard as in-person, plus: mode of delivery, who was present at the remote end, and any technical limitation that affected the session.

- Opa is fastest for "where do I find…" and "how does the practice handle…" questions.

# Lone Worker Safety Policy

## Purpose

Most Opal visits are conducted alone in other people's homes and community settings. This policy exists so that being alone never means being unaccounted for.

## Before the visit

1. Your calendar is your safety record: every community visit has an accurate address and time in the portal before it happens.
2. Review known risks for the setting: prior incidents, animals, household composition, access issues. New referrals with unknown environments warrant a phone conversation before the first visit.
3. If a specific risk is identified (history of aggression, volatile household), plan controls with the practice owner first — paired visits, public meeting places, or declining home visits are all legitimate outcomes.

## During the visit

- Park for easy exit; keep keys and phone on your person, not in a bag across the room.
- Position yourself with an exit path; do not allow yourself to be between a risk and a closed door.
- Trust discomfort. You may end any visit, at any point, without needing to justify the decision in the moment. Leave first, explain later.

## Check-ins

For standard metropolitan days, a finished calendar plus reachable phone is the baseline. For elevated-risk visits and all rural or remote travel, explicit check-in arrangements per the Rural and Remote Travel Policy apply: nominated contact, agreed check-in times, and an escalation step if a check-in is missed.

## After an incident or near miss

Report every incident and near miss — including "it was probably nothing" events — under the Incident Management Policy. Near-miss reports are how the next person stays safe.

**DRAFT — REQUIRES OPAL APPROVAL**

# Rural and Remote Travel Policy

## Purpose

Rural and remote trips carry risks that metropolitan practice does not: distance, isolation, patchy communications and environmental hazards. Planning is not bureaucracy; it is the treatment for those risks.

## Trip planning

1. Every rural or remote trip has a written trip plan before departure: route, stops, visit schedule, overnight arrangements, expected return, and the nominated check-in contact.
2. Complete the Pre-Trip Checklist (Resource Hub) for every trip. It is short deliberately, so it gets done.
3. Schedule realistically: driving fatigue is a primary hazard. No driving after a full clinical day where the drive exceeds two hours, without explicit agreement with the practice owner; overnight stays are the default for long circuits.

## Vehicle and equipment

- The vehicle is roadworthy, fuelled beyond the trip's needs, and carries water, first-aid kit and a charged power bank as minimum.
- For remote routes with poor mobile coverage, carry the practice's alternative communication device where issued, and know its use before departure. Coverage assumptions are checked, not guessed.

## Check-ins

- Agreed check-in times with the nominated contact, morning and end-of-day at minimum, plus on arrival at and departure from remote locations.
- A missed check-in triggers the escalation steps in the trip plan: attempted contact, then contact with the visit location, then emergency services with the trip plan's route details.

## Weather and conditions

Trips are postponed for severe weather warnings, road closures or fire danger affecting the route. A cancelled trip is a planning success, not a failure.

## Fatigue and wellbeing

Build travel days with breaks every two hours of driving. Fatigue self-assessment before the return leg is expected; staying overnight unplanned, with a phone call to the practice owner, is always the approved alternative to driving tired.

Professional Boundaries — A Practical Guide
description: Recognising and handling real boundary moments in community practice.
content:
# Professional Boundaries — A Practical Guide

The Professional Boundaries Policy sets the rules. This guide is about the moments — the specific, human situations where boundaries are actually tested in community practice.

## The cup of tea problem

You are in someone's home. Hospitality is offered. Accepting a cup of tea is usually relationship-building, not a violation — rigid refusal can itself be disrespectful, particularly in cultural contexts where hospitality matters. The line is not the tea; it is the drift. Staying for lunch, again, becoming the visit the family plans their day around socially — that is drift. Accept graciously, keep the session purposeful, and notice patterns.

## "Can I have your number?"

Families want direct access to someone they trust. The practical answer: "The practice number reaches me — I check messages every day, and anything urgent gets to me fast." You are not withholding care; you are protecting the sustainability of it, for them and for every other family.

## Gifts

A child's drawing: accept warmly, always. A box of chocolates at Christmas: accept, mention to the practice owner. Cash, expensive gifts, or anything that would embarrass you if disclosed: decline kindly — "It means a lot that you'd think of me, and the best thank-you is honestly just telling the practice."

## The friend request

Decline by policy, warmly: "I keep my socials personal — but I'd love to hear how things are going at our next session." In small communities where you already know the family, disclose the pre-existing relationship and plan with the practice owner.

## When you are the one drifting

Warning signs worth honest attention: making exceptions for one family, extending sessions socially, sharing your own problems, thinking about a participant's family outside work in a non-clinical way, or feeling reluctant to mention an interaction in supervision. That reluctance is the most reliable signal in this guide. Raise it in supervision while it is small — supervisors have heard it all before, and early conversations are routine maintenance, not confessions.

## Ending well

Boundaries include endings. Discharge is planned, communicated and clean: no informal "check-ins" that keep a therapeutic relationship alive off the books.

content:
# Assistive Technology Assessment Workflow

Assistive technology succeeds when it matches the person, the task and the environment — and fails expensively when any of the three is guessed. This workflow keeps the match honest.

## 1. Start from function, not catalogue

The referral is a functional problem ("cannot transfer safely", "cannot communicate wants at school"), not a product request. Even when a family arrives asking for a specific item, step back to the task and goal first — sometimes the requested item is right, and now you can say why.

## 2. Assess the person-task-environment triangle

- **Person:** relevant capacities and constraints — physical, sensory, cognitive, and importantly preferences and tolerance. Equipment that embarrasses its user becomes garage equipment.
- **Task:** exactly what needs doing, where it breaks down, and what level of independence is the goal.
- **Environment(s):** every setting the AT must work in — measure doorways, transport, storage, and consider every user (a hoist has carers as users too).

## 3. Consider the low-tech option first

The credibility of every AT recommendation rests on the simpler options having been genuinely considered. Task modification, routine change, off-the-shelf items — document what was considered and why it does or does not suffice. This is also the value-for-money reasoning funders rightly expect.

## 4. Shortlist and involve suppliers appropriately

Shortlist candidate solutions on clinical grounds before supplier involvement. Suppliers bring product knowledge worth having; prescription decisions remain clinical and conflict-free (see the Conflict of Interest Policy — no commissions, options offered where reasonable).

## 5. Trial in the real environment

A trial in the home, school or community setting where the AT must work — not the showroom. Use the Equipment Trial Guide: define success measures before the trial starts, involve the daily users, run it long enough to expose real-life friction, and record outcomes against the measures.

## 6. Decide, and write the justification

The recommendation follows Clinical Recommendations structure: the functional need, options considered, trial outcomes, the selected solution with specifications, training and maintenance needs, and expected participation outcomes. Cost information is quoted from supplier quotes, and claiming or funding pathways are checked against current official guidance — never asserted from memory, never guaranteed.

## 7. Plan implementation, training and review

Delivery is the midpoint, not the end: fitting and setup, training for the participant and everyone who supports the AT's use, integration into routines, and a scheduled review — because bodies, tasks and environments change. Record who owns maintenance and what the escalation path is when something breaks in week one, which is when things break.

## Safety boundaries

Complex seating, pressure care surfaces, home modifications with structural implications and high-risk transfers equipment have specialist dimensions — involve or refer to appropriately experienced clinicians rather than stretching. See Wheelchair and Seating, Pressure Management and Home Modifications for where those lines sit.

content:
# Australian OT Competency Standards (2018)

The Occupational Therapy Board of Australia's competency standards describe the threshold competence expected of every registered occupational therapist. They took effect on 1 January 2019 and are organised into four areas.

## 1. Professionalism

Ethical, lawful, culturally safe practice: acting within scope, maintaining boundaries and confidentiality, obtaining informed consent, and practising in a way that is culturally safe for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and all communities.

**What this means at Opal**

- The policy suite (privacy, consent, boundaries, documentation) is this competency area, operationalised — acknowledging and following it is competency evidence, not paperwork.
- Cultural safety is a practice skill we develop deliberately, especially for rural and remote work. See Cultural Safety and Respectful Practice.
- Scope questions go to supervision early. Working at the edge of scope with support is growth; working beyond it alone is a breach.

## 2. Knowledge and Learning

Current knowledge of occupational therapy theory and evidence, and a commitment to lifelong learning and reflective practice.

**What this means at Opal**

- CPD is planned against these standards, tracked in the portal, and reviewed in supervision — see the CPD Policy.
- Evidence-informed practice is expected: know why you chose the approach you chose. See the Evidence-Informed Practice guide.

## 3. Occupational Therapy Process and Practice

Partnering with clients through assessment, goal setting, intervention and review, with occupation at the centre.

**What this means at Opal**

- Assessments produce functional findings, not test scores alone — see Writing Functional Impact.
- Goals are the participant's, in their words, with therapy goals built underneath — see the Goal Writing guide.
- Review is honest: interventions that are not working change.

## 4. Communication

Clear, respectful, effective communication with clients, families and teams, including written communication that serves its reader.

**What this means at Opal**

- Notes and reports meet the Clinical Documentation Standard: person-first, specific, readable by the participant.
- We communicate proactively with schools, families and other providers within consent — silence is where care coordination fails.

title: Cognitive Assessment — Overview
description: The OT contribution to understanding cognition in daily function.
content:
# Cognitive Assessment — Overview

Occupational therapy's cognitive assessment question is functional: how does this person's thinking support or limit what they need and want to do? We assess cognition-in-occupation, complementing — never duplicating — neuropsychological assessment.

## Scope and boundaries

- OT cognitive assessment informs support planning, safety decisions and intervention design. Diagnostic questions, capacity determinations with legal weight, and detailed cognitive profiling belong with the appropriate specialists — contribute to them, do not substitute for them.
- Use standardised cognitive screens and functional cognitive assessments only within your training and the tool's licensing (see the Assessment Tool Directory).

## The functional method

1. **Occupation as the test.** Observe multi-step real tasks — meal preparation is the classic — and record where cognition shows itself: following the sequence, handling interruption, safety judgement, error detection and correction, adapting when an ingredient is missing.
2. **Vary support and structure.** Performance with a written list versus without; with prompting versus alone. The support-performance gap is the finding.
3. **Triangulate.** Informants describe the pattern across weeks — missed medications, repeated questions, lost bills — that one visit cannot show. Recent changes matter more than absolute level.
4. **Context and confounds.** Fatigue, pain, low mood, hearing, language and anxiety all masquerade as cognitive impairment. Note them, and time assessment fairly.

## Safety findings act fast

Cognitive findings with immediate safety weight — stove use, medication management, driving, wandering — are not filed for the report. Address interim safety with the person and family the same day, and escalate per the Clinical Escalation Pathway where risk is urgent.

## What You'll Learn

- What each calendar view is best for
- How to read event tiles, statuses and locations
- How to move between days, weeks and months quickly

## Before You Start

Complete Getting Started with the Opal Portal. If you use Outlook, connect it first so the calendar shows your whole day.

## Steps

1. Open Calendar. The Week view loads by default and shows your full week at a glance.
2. Switch to Day view for a single day in detail — best on busy community days with tight travel.
3. Switch to Month view to scan ahead for report deadlines, leave and quieter weeks.
4. Click any event tile to see its details: time, client, location, session type and status.
5. Use the mini month in the sidebar to jump to any date, and the arrows to step forwards or backwards.
6. Note the colour and status conventions: cancelled sessions are visibly distinct and travel blocks sit between visits.

## Common Problems

- **An event seems missing** — check you are on the right week, then check whether it was cancelled; cancelled events render differently rather than disappearing.

title: Routine Development
description: Building daily routines that hold — for families and adults alike.
content:
# Routine Development

Routines are load-bearing structures: they convert effortful decisions into automatic sequence, freeing capacity for what cannot be automated. Building them is a core, underrated OT intervention.

## Principles

1. **One routine at a time.** The household that needs five new routines gets them one by one, each stable before the next begins. Parallel routine-building fails in proportion to its ambition.
2. **Anchor to what already happens.** New steps attach to existing fixed points — after the kettle, before the school bus. Free-floating routines drift; anchored ones hold.
3. **Design with, not for.** The family's actual constraints — shift work, shared care arrangements, small kitchens, low-energy evenings — are design inputs, not compliance problems. A routine that ignores the household's reality is a worksheet, not an intervention.
4. **Make it visible.** Externalise the sequence where it runs: picture schedule at child height, checklist on the fridge, phone alarms for the adult version. Visibility carries the routine through low-capacity days.
5. **Rehearse to boring.** Walk it through together, at low-stakes times, until it needs no thought. Expect two to six weeks of support before a routine holds on its own — plan the coaching cadence accordingly.

## When routines break

They will — holidays, illness, a house move. Normalise breakage in advance and script the restart: back to the visual, back to the anchor, no blame. A family that knows how to restart a routine owns it; one that thinks breakage is failure abandons it.

## Flexibility is part of the build

Routines serve people, not the reverse. Build in the acceptable variations (the two-breakfast menu, the wet-weather option) so that flexibility is inside the routine rather than a breach of it — especially important where change tolerance is itself a clinical goal.

title: Functional Observation
description: Skilled observation of real task performance — the core OT assessment method.
content:
# Functional Observation

Skilled observation of a person doing a real task in a real setting is occupational therapy's signature assessment method — often more decision-relevant than any score.

## Set it up honestly

- Observe the actual occupation in its actual context: breakfast in the kitchen it happens in, writing at the school desk, the transfer in the real bathroom.
- Minimise your distortion of the scene: brief the person, position unobtrusively, resist helping. The performance you want is the one that happens without you.
- One task observed well beats four skimmed. Plan what you must see against the referral question.

## What to record

- **Task sequence and breakdown points** — where exactly performance falters: initiation, sequencing, a physical demand, a decision point.
- **Prompt levels** — what input restored performance (none, gesture, verbal, demonstration, physical assistance) and how often.
- **Time and fatigue** — duration, pace changes, quality decay across the task.
- **Compensations** — the workarounds the person has built; they are both assessment findings and intervention assets.
- **Safety events and near misses** — factually, with context.
- **The person's own commentary** — quoted; how the task feels from inside is data observation cannot reach.

## Interpretation discipline

Record observation first, interpretation second, visibly separated (see Clinical Note Quality). One observation is a sample, not a verdict — note the conditions (time of day, who was present, a good day or bad day by report) and triangulate with informants before generalising.

title: Executive Function Assessment — Overview
description: A quick-reference method for assessing EF in daily life.
content:
# Executive Function Assessment — Overview

A condensed method companion to Executive Functioning — Understanding and Assessment. Use that guide for the full picture; use this as the checklist.

## The four moves

1. **Real multi-step task, observed.** Cooking, packing, planning an outing. Record the exact breakdown point: initiation, plan, sequence, distraction, error recovery. The breakdown point is the treatment target.
2. **Vary the conditions.** Same task with structure versus without; prompted versus independent; preferred versus non-preferred. The gap between conditions is the clinical finding — and the funding-relevant one.
3. **Get the week-scale picture.** Informant and self-report of daily life: mornings, deadlines, bills, appointments. Standardised EF questionnaires within competence and licensing add structure (see the Assessment Tool Directory).
4. **Find the intact machinery.** Interests that summon sustained attention, routines that run reliably, environments where performance normalises. Intervention will be built from these.

## Reporting reminders

- Re-describe character words from the referral ("lazy", "defiant") as function, with evidence.
- Prompt levels and support-performance gaps, stated numerically where possible.
- Run the chain: impairment → functional impact → participation consequence → support requirement.
- State-dependence noted: stress, fatigue and interest change EF performance, and the assessment should say under which conditions it sampled.

title: Wheelchair and Seating — Overview
description: High-level orientation, with clear deferral to specialist assessment.
content:
# Wheelchair and Seating — Overview

Wheelchair and seating provision is a specialist area within occupational therapy. This overview orients generalist clinicians to the territory — and is explicit about its boundary: **complex wheelchair and seating prescription is deferred to clinicians with specific competence in seating assessment.** Getting this wrong causes pressure injuries, postural deterioration and abandoned equipment.

## Why seating is different

A wheelchair is not one decision but a system of them: mobility base, seating and postural supports, pressure management, transport compatibility, environment fit and growth or change over time. The interactions are where the risk lives — a cushion choice affects posture, which affects function, which affects pressure distribution.

## What a generalist can and should do

1. **Recognise need early.** Flag deteriorating posture, discomfort, skin changes, reduced sitting tolerance, or equipment the person has outgrown — early referral protects months of function.
2. **Contribute the functional picture.** The seating specialist needs exactly what we do well: how the person spends their day, the tasks the chair must serve, every environment it must work in, transfers, transport and the goals that matter.
3. **Check the basics on review visits.** Is the equipment being used as set up? Are supports where they were fitted? Any skin concerns reported (escalate immediately — see Pressure Management)? Is anything broken or outgrown?
4. **Coordinate.** Own the referral, the information flow with consent, and the follow-through — specialist assessment works best inside a well-coordinated episode.

## What is deferred to specialist assessment

- Prescription of complex manual or powered wheelchairs and configured seating systems.
- Postural assessment for custom or configured supports.
- Pressure risk assessment where risk is elevated or a history of pressure injury exists.
- Scripting changes to existing complex systems.

"Deferred" means genuinely handed to, or jointly conducted with, a clinician with seating competence — not rubber-stamped.

## Red flags for immediate action

Skin redness or breakdown related to sitting, new pain in sitting, sudden postural change, or equipment failure affecting safety: act the same day — escalate per the Clinical Escalation Pathway, involve the specialist and supplier, and document.

# Consent Policy

## Purpose

Consent at Opal is informed, specific, documented and revisited — not a signature collected once and forgotten.

## What informed consent requires

Before services begin, the participant (or their decision-maker where one is lawfully in place) understands, in language accessible to them:

- what the service involves and what it aims to achieve;
- fees, funding source and cancellation terms;
- how their information is used and who may see it (see the Privacy and Confidentiality Policy);
- their right to decline, withdraw or change their mind at any time without penalty to the therapeutic relationship.

## Specific consents

Separate, explicit consent is obtained for: photographs or recordings; telehealth delivery; use of approved recording or transcription tools in sessions; sharing information with schools, other providers or family members outside the decision-making arrangement; and student or observer presence.

## Capacity and supported decision-making

Adults are presumed to have capacity. Where capacity is in doubt, support the person's own decision-making first; substitute decision-making arrangements (guardianship, nominee) are verified, not assumed. Requirements vary by jurisdiction: Requires legal/regulatory verification.

## Children and young people

Consent involves those with parental responsibility, and the child's own assent is sought in an age-appropriate way. Family law arrangements affecting consent are recorded and respected.

## Recording and revisiting

Consent is documented in the clinical record at commencement, when the service changes materially, and whenever the participant's circumstances suggest it should be revisited. Withdrawal of consent is actioned immediately and documented.

description: What to do, in order, when clinical risk exceeds your comfort or scope.
content:
# Clinical Escalation Pathway

Use this pathway whenever a clinical situation exceeds your confidence, competence or scope — or whenever safety is in question. Escalating is expected behaviour, not an admission of failure.

## Level 1 — Immediate danger

If a participant, family member or you are in immediate danger: call 000 first. Move to safety. Then phone the practice owner. Document afterwards, the same day.

## Level 2 — Urgent clinical risk (same day)

Examples: disclosure of harm or abuse, acute deterioration, medication concerns, unsafe equipment in active use, threats of self-harm.

1. Make the situation as safe as you reasonably can without exceeding your scope.
2. Phone the practice owner (or your supervisor if directed) before leaving the setting where practicable.
3. Follow their direction on notifications — mandatory reporting obligations may apply. Where obligations depend on registration status or jurisdiction: Requires legal/regulatory verification.
4. Record a factual, timed incident note the same day and complete an incident report per the Incident Management Policy.

## Level 3 — Non-urgent clinical concern

Examples: slow deterioration, family conflict affecting therapy, uncertainty about assessment findings, scope-of-practice doubt.

1. Note the concern in the clinical record.
2. Raise it at the next supervision session, or sooner by message if it cannot wait a week.
3. Agree and document the plan that comes out of supervision.

## Always

- Phone beats message for anything urgent. Never discharge an urgent concern into an email and consider it handled.
- If two levels seem plausible, act at the higher one.
- If a mandatory reporting question arises, do not resolve it alone — escalate and verify. Requires legal/regulatory verification.

# Supervision Policy

## Purpose

Supervision is how we protect participants, develop clinicians and keep isolated community practice connected. It is planned, protected time — not a corridor conversation.

## Structure

1. **Frequency.** New graduates and new starters: weekly for the first three months, then reviewed. Experienced clinicians: at least fortnightly, with frequency reviewed against caseload complexity.
2. **Protected.** Supervision sessions are scheduled in the calendar and are not routinely cancelled for operational pressure. A cancelled session is rebooked within the week.
3. **Documented.** Each session records topics discussed, decisions made and actions agreed. Clinical decisions arising from supervision are reflected in the relevant clinical records.

## Content

Supervision covers clinical reasoning and case review, risk and escalation, professional development against the Australian OT competency standards, wellbeing and workload, and boundary or ethical questions. Supervisees bring cases; supervisors bring structure and challenge.

## Responsibilities

- **Supervisees** prepare, raise concerns early (especially risk, boundary and scope issues), and action what is agreed.
- **Supervisors** provide a psychologically safe space, keep records, and escalate to the practice owner where participant safety requires it — supervision is confidential, but not at the price of safety.

## CPD linkage

Supervision that meets the OT Board's definitions may count towards CPD, including interactive hours. Record it in your CPD log with reflections. See the CPD Policy and current registration standard.

content:
# NDIS Practice Standards — What They Are and How Opal Uses Them

## Who they formally apply to

The NDIS Practice Standards **formally apply to registered NDIS providers** — they are the benchmark against which registered providers are audited. Nothing in this resource implies that Opal Therapy is a registered NDIS provider; registration status is a matter of fact confirmed by the practice owner, and obligations that turn on it require verification: Requires legal/regulatory verification.

## Why we read them anyway

Opal chooses to use the Practice Standards as an **internal quality benchmark**. They are a well-constructed description of what good, safe service provision looks like, and holding ourselves against a standard we are not compelled to meet is cheap insurance and honest practice.

## The shape of the Standards

The core module covers four broad areas:

1. **Rights and responsibilities** — person-centred supports, individual values and beliefs, privacy and dignity, independence and informed choice, freedom from violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation and discrimination.
2. **Governance and operational management** — governance arrangements, risk and incident management, complaints, human resources, continuity of supports.
3. **Provision of supports** — access, planning, service agreements, responsive support provision, transitions.
4. **Support provision environment** — safe environment, participant money and property, management of medication and waste where relevant.

Supplementary modules address higher-risk supports (for example specialist behaviour support and high-intensity daily personal activities) that sit outside Opal's current scope.

## Using them at Opal

- When reviewing a policy or process, ask: would this satisfy the corresponding Practice Standard outcome? If not, why not?
- Quality gaps identified against the Standards go into the same review loop as incidents and complaints.
